title: Understanding CORS and the Same-Origin Policy
description: Learn why browsers restrict cross-origin requests and how CORS relaxes those rules.

data.text: Browsers enforce a security rule called the same-origin policy. Two URLs share the same origin only when their protocol, host (domain), and port are all identical. If any of those three parts differ, the browser treats the request as cross-origin and blocks the response by default.

terms.definition: The combination of protocol, host, and port (for example, https://example.com:443).
A browser rule that prevents a page from reading data loaded from a different origin.
Any request sent to a different origin than the page that initiated it.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — a W3C standard that lets servers opt-in to sharing resources with specific origins.

data.title: Why Does the Browser Do This?
data.text: The same-origin policy prevents malicious websites from silently reading sensitive data from another site you are logged into. Without it, any random site could make a request to your banking app and read the response.

Imagine a frontend app running on https://frontend.example.com that tries to fetch data from https://api.example.com. Even though both sites belong to the same company, the browser sees different origins because the subdomains differ. Without CORS, the browser blocks the response and the JavaScript code cannot read the data.

The browser sends the request, but when the response arrives it checks for a special header: Access-Control-Allow-Origin. If that header is missing or does not match the requesting origin, the browser discards the response and raises a CORS error in the console.

data.caption: How the browser enforces the same-origin policy
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser as Browser (frontend)
    participant Server as API Server
    Browser->>Server: GET /api/data (cross-origin)
    Server-->>Browser: 200 OK + JSON body
    Note right of Browser: Checks for Access-Control-Allow-Origin header
    Browser-->>Browser: Header missing or mismatch? Block the response.

data.text: CORS is a server-side mechanism. The server includes specific HTTP headers in its responses to tell the browser: "I allow these origins to read my data." Once the browser sees a matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, it releases the response to the JavaScript code.

cards.title: Without CORS
cards.description: The server returns data but the browser blocks JavaScript from reading it.

cards.title: With CORS
cards.description: The server explicitly allows trusted origins, and the browser permits the response.
pros: Fine-grained control over who can access data

data.title: Spot the Cross-Origin Request
data.description: Determine whether each request is same-origin or cross-origin.
steps: Page origin: https://app.example.com. Request: https://app.example.com/users. Is this cross-origin?
Page origin: https://app.example.com. Request: https://api.example.com/users. Is this cross-origin?
Page origin: https://example.com. Request: https://example.com:8443/api. Is this cross-origin?
Page origin: https://example.com. Request: https://example.com/api. Is this cross-origin?
data.expectedOutcome: You should identify that only requests with the exact same protocol, host, and port are same-origin. Any difference makes it cross-origin.

items.text: I can explain the three parts of an origin (protocol, host, port)
I understand why browsers enforce the same-origin policy
I know what header the browser looks for to allow a cross-origin response
I can tell whether two URLs share the same origin

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The same-origin policy restricts pages from reading responses from different origins
Origins are defined by protocol, host, and port
CORS is a server-side opt-in that relaxes the same-origin policy
The browser looks for Access-Control-Allow-Origin on every cross-origin response
data.takeaway: Next, you will learn exactly how to enable CORS in an ASP.NET Core application.
